title: the seasons
hook: frost on the windshield and a bigger appetite: Charaka's chapter on the seasons has a reason for both

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seasons: a year in two halves, adana, the taking, and visarga, the giving. Did the season take something from you, and did you give one small thing back? Day one thousand three hundred two.

Frost on a car windshield before work. Breath you can see. And by lunch, a hunger that feels bigger than it did in the summer, as if the body quietly raised its order. A bowl of something hot tastes better than it has any right to. That's usually filed under comfort food and left there. But one of Ayurveda's classical texts, the Charaka Samhita, gives the cold months a careful reading, and the bigger appetite sits right at the center of it. This week has walked from oil and movement and good conduct out to the year itself. Today, the cold.
screen: `FROST ON THE WINDSHIELD.` → `A BIGGER APPETITE.` → `TODAY, THE COLD.`

segments.voice: Charaka's chapter on the seasons names two winters. Hemanta, early winter. Shishira, late winter, colder and harsher. And here's the observation it builds on, paraphrased. In the cold, the body's fire of digestion is held in by the cold outside, and it grows strong. Strong enough to handle heavy, substantial food. Then a sharper line. If that strong fire isn't given proper food, the text says, it turns on the body's own tissues. So winter, in this picture, isn't the season for skimping. The chapter's advice is warm and generous: substantial food with some richness to it, warm water, oil rubbed into the skin, the way this week's oil day described, heavy clothes, warm rooms, the sun when it's out. Three things follow. First, it's the rule from the dosha days again: like increases like, the opposite brings it down. Cold is met with warmth, the dry winter air with oil. Second, the appetite isn't treated as a fault to fight. It's read as the body doing its job in the cold, and the job is to feed it well. Third, the calendar of festivals sits close by. In parts of India, at Makar Sankranti in the middle of winter, people share sweets of sesame and jaggery, and in Maharashtra they say, roughly, take this sweet and speak sweetly. Winter food at a winter festival, given away. None of this asks you to live in an Indian winter. It asks you to look at the season you're actually in, and answer it.
screen: `HEMANTA AND SHISHIRA, THE COLD MONTHS` · `A STRONG FIRE IN THE COLD` · `FEED IT, OR IT FEEDS ON YOU` · `SESAME AND JAGGERY AT SANKRANTI`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the warmth you already have. Sit, and let the breath settle. Look for the warmest place in the body right now: maybe the hands folded in your lap, maybe the chest, maybe the belly. Rest your attention there. Feel the out-breath, warm as it leaves. If there's cold somewhere, at the feet or the back of the neck, notice it too, at the edges, without fixing it. Warmth in the middle, weather at the edges. If you pray, you can give thanks for the last warm meal you ate. The bell holds the time.
The seasons. In winter, Charaka's reading is a strong inner fire held in by the cold, one that needs real food. Today's word.
Your line: the seasons. Today, meet the weather with its opposite once: something warm against the cold, or something cooling if it's hot where you are. Day one thousand three hundred two.

howItsDone: People who follow Ayurveda adjust food and habits through the year as the classical texts describe; in the cold months that means substantial warm food, oil on the skin and warm clothing, and in parts of India families share sesame-and-jaggery sweets at Makar Sankranti.
